messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Parole Officer
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Stress: Stress, Somatic (Heart Racing): Own heart racing or pounding
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
  Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Rodrigo

Rodrigo Hernández had been a parole officer for twenty-three years when the incident happened. He had built a reputation for fairness—tough but principled, the kind of officer who could sit down with a man fresh out of prison and see something worth salvaging. His colleagues respected him. His parolees, many of them, actually listened to him. He had come to believe that his job was to enforce the law while holding onto the possibility that people could change. That belief had become the architecture of his life.

On a humid afternoon in June, Rodrigo was conducting a home visit in a neighborhood where three of his cases lived. He had parked his unmarked sedan on the corner, and as he approached the apartment building, he noticed Officer Delgado—a patrol officer he had known casually for years—standing outside with his hand on his duty belt. Rodrigo raised his hand in greeting. What happened next occurred in fragments that his mind still refuses to assemble into a coherent whole. There was shouting. Someone—not Rodrigo—had a gun. Delgado moved toward Rodrigo, and then Rodrigo felt the impact, a blow to his ribs so violent it drove the air from his lungs. He fell. There was more shouting, and then Delgado was on top of him, striking his face, his shoulders, his arms as Rodrigo tried to shield himself. When it ended, Rodrigo was bleeding from a gash above his eye, his ribs screaming, and Delgado was being pulled away by other officers who had arrived. The story that emerged was a terrible mistake: Delgado had been responding to a call about an armed robbery suspect in the area. He had seen Rodrigo approaching and, in a moment of catastrophic confusion, thought he was the suspect. The department's internal investigation found that Delgado had acted recklessly but without malice. No charges were filed. Delgado was suspended for two weeks.

In the months after, Rodrigo began to notice that his body had become a stranger to him. His heart would race without warning—sometimes in his office, sometimes at home—and he would grip the edge of his desk or the kitchen counter, certain that something terrible was about to happen. He found himself unable to enter silence without dread. When his wife, Maria, would sit beside him in the evening without speaking, he would feel his shoulders tense, his breath shallow. The quiet felt pregnant with danger, as though violence itself lived in the space between words. At the office, he started scanning the hallways before he moved through them, noting exits, watching hands, tracking the position of everyone around him. His colleagues began to comment that he seemed distracted, that he had become rigid in his interactions.

The memory itself had become slippery. Rodrigo could recall the heat of that afternoon, the moment he raised his hand to greet Delgado, but when he tried to hold the rest of it in his mind—the sequence of blows, the sound of his own voice—it dissolved like something too extreme to be real. He found himself pushing it away before he could examine it fully, as though looking at it directly would shatter something essential in him. The worst part was not what he remembered but what was missing. He knew he had been beaten, but entire sections of the event had simply vanished. Sometimes he wondered if he was exaggerating it in his mind, if he had imagined some of it, because surely something that violent would leave a complete memory, not these fragmentary, unreliable pieces.

What had broken him most completely was not the violence itself but the betrayal. Delgado was a cop. Rodrigo was a cop. They inhabited the same world, followed the same code. And when the system that was supposed to hold Delgado accountable—the investigation, the department—had essentially shrugged and moved on, Rodrigo felt the ground shift beneath him. The institution that had been his home for nearly a quarter-century had failed him utterly. No charges. Two weeks' suspension. The injustice of it sat in his chest like a stone. He had spent his career believing in accountability, in consequences, in the possibility of redemption through the system. Now he understood that the system protected its own, and he was not protected.

For months, Rodrigo continued to work. He conducted his parole visits, filed his reports, sat across from men trying to rebuild their lives. But he had begun to avoid situations where he might encounter other officers. He would take longer routes to avoid the precinct. When people misbehaved—when a parolee missed an appointment, when someone cut him off in traffic—he felt a surge of rage so intense it frightened him, as though all the injustice he could not direct at the system was pouring into these smaller moments. Maria had noticed the change. She had stopped trying to sit with him in the evenings. His supervisor had asked him, carefully, if he was all right.

It was his daughter, calling from out of state, saying she was worried about how he sounded on the phone, that made Rodrigo finally admit that something was profoundly wrong. He had come to believe that he could not trust the world to be fair, that danger lurked in silence and in the hands of people he thought he knew, that his own mind could not be trusted to remember what had happened to him. He made an appointment with a therapist, sitting in the waiting room with his jaw clenched, wondering if talking about it would make it real or make it disappear entirely.
